**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 1**

For the initial phase, each of the six proposed sites will log hourly air-temperature, wind speed/direction, barometric pressure, and cumulative rainfall, recorded in a bound logbook with timestamp, observer initials, sky-condition code, and instrument serial number; before the first hourly entry the temperature probe is cross-checked against a NIST-traceable reference thermometer to confirm it sits within ±0.2 °C. To guard against a concrete failure—systematic thermal bias from mounting the sensor on a sun-facing concrete ledge, which in a mid-July afternoon could inflate readings by 3–5 °C relative to true ambient and corrupt the weekly trend—I require the Stevenson screen to hang at least 1.5 m from any vertical surface, with a 360° open-sky view verified by a simple horizon sketch logged at installation. Each Saturday's compiled summary will be compared against the nearest national (NOAA/NCDC) station, and any residual offset beyond combined instrument uncertainty (±0.5 °C) will trigger a recalibration entry rather than a silent correction.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 2**

I adopt your 1.5 m Stevenson standoff, the horizon-sketch verification, and the ±0.5 °C recalibration trigger verbatim; they close the two most probable temperature-integrity holes. For the missing-data gap you haven't yet named, a missed hour is logged "MISSING" (never interpolated) and three consecutive gaps trigger a formal site-replacement review; each station must also sit ≥50 m from a paved roadway so exhaust heat and tire aerosol cannot bias the barometer or truncate anemometer readings. The concrete failure this guards against: placing the cup anemometer on the south face of a two-storey roof embeds it in a chimney wake that at 2 m s⁻¹ true speed—a neighbourhood-gust regime—under-reads by 20–30 %, so the mast must clear every obstruction by at least twice its height in all azimuths, verified with the same horizon-sketch you specified. The weekly public report will therefore carry a per-site data-completeness percentage, and any site below 62 % completeness (≈90 % of available hours) is flagged "provisional" in the bulletin rather than silently smoothed into the trend.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 3**

I accept the wake-clearance rule and the 62 % completeness flag without modification; they keep the weekly bulletin honest without forcing us to discard a season of data. For the gauge variable you have left open, each site will carry a 20-inch standard rain gauge with a self-cleaning wiper at 1.0 m above mown grass, supplemented in winter by a graduated-cylinder secondary read at 02:00 to capture frozen accumulation that no tipping-bucket threshold can resolve. The failure this guards against is unglamorous but persistent: a single evergreen bough overhanging the inlet by only 15° intercepts enough light-rain droplets to shave roughly 15 % off every event, so a true monthly total of 60 mm is logged as ≈51 mm and the neighborhood's comparison column quietly trends low against the NOAA station. I therefore require the same 360° horizon-sketch at installation for the rain inlet, with any bough within 30° of the rim annotated and a pruning-or-relocation note entered before the first forecast snowfall.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 4**

I adopt the bough-annotation rule and the 02:00 graduated-cylinder procedure; without that winter secondary read a snowpack that hoards and later releases four millimetres overnight would surface as a phantom 0.4 mm/hr rate in the hourly log, exactly the kind of artifact your pruning note is meant to eliminate. For the pressure variable you listed but have not yet instrumented, each site will carry a sealed aneroid module (0.1 hPa resolution) calibrated monthly against a NIST-traceable portable barometer, and every reading is reduced to mean-sea level using the site's surveyed elevation and a temperature-corrected lapse rate before the weekly comparison column is populated. The failure this guards against is mundane but diagnostic: if Site 3, sitting eighteen metres above Site 1, simply logs raw station pressure and the compiler forgets the MSL correction, the bulletin shows a persistent ≈1.5 hPa "high" at Site 3 that mimics a blocked-ridge signature and poisons the cross-site coherence check. I therefore require that any inter-site pressure spread exceeding 0.5 hPa after MSL reduction triggers an automatic elevation-recording audit—a repeat GPS survey of the affected site—rather than a silent averaging across the six columns.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 5**

I adopt the MSL-reduction and 0.5 hPa inter-site spread rule, but I replace the hourly comparison column with a weekly-mean comparison against the nearest NOAA/NCDC station, requiring two consecutive weeks of exceedance beyond ±0.3 hPa (pressure) or ±0.5 °C (temperature) before any audit is ordered. The failure this prevents is operable and tempting: in convective season a single localized storm cell parked over the NOAA station but 4 km short of your neighborhood produces a transient 1.5–2 hPa hourly spike, and if the compiler flags every hourly deviation, observers learn within three weeks to treat the audit alert as noise and ignore the next genuine aneroid drift. The weekly bulletin will therefore carry a single combined expanded-uncertainty figure per variable—0.1 hPa instrument resolution, 0.1 hPa residual six-week calibration drift, 0.2 hPa lapse-rate error under a stable inversion (the worst realistic case for an 18 m elevation differential), and a site-specific microclimate constant estimated once at installation and subtracted as a bias term—yielding ≈±0.3 hPa at 95 % confidence, which is exactly the two-week tolerance above and closes the loop between what you log, what you compare, and what a reader may legitimately conclude from the bulletin.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 6**

I adopt the weekly-mean comparison, the two-week persistence gate, and your ≈±0.3 hPa expanded-uncertainty budget verbatim; they convert the pressure column from an hourly alarm feed into a defensible trend product and remove the exact convective-spike false positive that would have burned observer trust by week four. For the wind variable still lacking an instrument specification, each site will mount a three-cup anemometer with a heated, self-starting bearing (start threshold ≤ 0.5 m s⁻¹) at 10 m AGL, sampling a 10-minute mean speed and a 10-minute median direction logged as 360° azimuth reduced to a 16-point compass before entry; the ten-minute window is non-negotiable because the neighborhood's prevailing regime of 1–4 m s⁻¹ sits squarely in the cup-stall zone where a three-second averager locks and releases in steps. The concrete failure this prevents: during a calm March night, Site 4's anemometer stalls at 0.0 m s⁻¹ from bearing friction while Site 5, one kilometre east and slightly exposed, legitimately reads 2.8 m s⁻¹, and a naïve reader of the weekly wind-rose infers a spurious local pressure gradient reversal that no pressure-column check can refute because both aneroids sit within tolerance. I therefore require that any site logging more than 30 % zero-sped entries in a seven-day window triggers the same formal review your three-consecutive-missing-hour rule already mandates, and the weekly bulletin prints the percentage of non-zero wind entries alongside the completeness figure so a reader can weigh the wind-rose before drawing any circulation conclusion.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 7**

I adopt the heated-bearing specification, the ten-minute averaging window, and the thirty-percent zero-speed review trigger without modification; they close the bearing-friction hole cleanly. For the bulletin's cross-site summary row, I require that the "neighborhood consensus" wind entry be computed as the component-wise median of the U and V vectors across all sites meeting the sixty-two-percent completeness threshold, never as a median of scalar speed or of compass bearing. The failure this prevents: during a katabatic episode in early April, Sites 1–3 on the valley floor log 3.2 m/s from 270° while Sites 5–6 on the upper slope log 2.1 m/s from 090°, and a naïve median-bearing calculation falls at 180°—the geometric gap—printing a westerly vector that matches no site and implying a phantom valley convergence that, paired with a flat pressure column, reads to a lay reader as a stalled front. I therefore mandate that whenever the inter-site directional spread exceeds ninety degrees, the consensus cell is printed as "SPLIT" with both mode vectors displayed side-by-side and the NOAA comparison cell for that variable left blank for the week rather than populated with the gap value.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 8**

I adopt the component-wise U/V median, the ninety-degree SPLIT threshold, and the blanked NOAA comparison cell verbatim; they prevent the valley-katabatic phantom-convergence reading without sacrificing the week's otherwise-valid scalar-speed context. For the instrument-retirement question your serial-number requirement implies but has not yet regulated, every replacement of a Stevenson screen, anemometer, or aneroid module must carry a fourteen-day co-residence overlap in which old and new units log the same hour, the one-time differential is entered as a bridging line keyed to both serial numbers, and the expanded-uncertainty budget for that site's temperature (or pressure) column is temporarily widened by the bridging term until the next monthly NIST cross-check confirms the replacement sits within ±0.2 °C. The concrete failure this guards against: Site 2's thermistor housing corrodes after fourteen months, the replacement carries a +0.15 °C factory zero-offset, and if the compiler swaps the serial number without a bridging entry the weekly-mean column steps −0.15 °C, persisting into week two and tripping your two-week persistence gate on a phantom cooling trend that would send a crew to audit a perfectly healthy pressure column. I therefore mandate that no bridging line older than thirty days may be retired from the audit trail, and that any week during which a site operates without its paired instrument logged under the old serial number prints a bold "BRIDGE PENDING" annotation in the bulletin header so a reader never mistakes a one-week instrumental artifact for a neighbourhood-scale shift.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 9**

I adopt the fourteen-day overlap, the bridging-line rule, and the bold "BRIDGE PENDING" header annotation verbatim; they make the replacement window auditable without reopening the two-week persistence gate. For the reporting question your audit-trail requirement implies but has not yet regulated, every weekly bulletin will carry a SHA-256 hash of the compiled dataset, and a permanent public-appendix section—accessible to any resident by request—where horizon-sketch scans, elevation-survey records, bridging lines, and errata are filed in serial-number order alongside the bound logbook. The concrete failure this guards against: a well-meaning volunteer "corrects" a transcription slip (18.4 → 18.5 °C) directly in the compiled file without entering an erratum line, so the archived logbook and eleven successive printed bulletins diverge by 0.1 °C, and when a resident in year two pulls the bound logbook to verify a cooling trend the quiet discrepancy reads as fabrication and strips the project of its public-credibility anchor. I therefore mandate that any post-compilation edit requires a two-initials erratum entry in the bound logbook and a superseding bulletin issued within five working days, printed with the prior hash struck through and the revised hash alongside, so the audit trail and the bulletin can never silently desynchronize.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 10**

I adopt the SHA-256 hash sealing, the two-initials erratum mandate, and the five-day superseding-bulletin-with-struck-through-prior-hash rule verbatim; they make the audit trail tamper-evident without reopening the weekly comparison tolerances. The upstream gap your transcription-slip example exposes is that the hash protects the compiled file only after compilation, so a single-digit transposition introduced at the keyboard survives indefinitely inside a cryptographically valid dataset; I therefore mandate that the observer who wrote the bound-logbook entry is never the same person who keys that entry into the compiled spreadsheet, and that each Monday's digitisation session includes a five-entry random spot-audit per site in which the transcriber re-reads the logbook page aloud and a second initial verifies the typed digit before the file is frozen and hashed. The concrete failure this closes: at Site 3's 02:00 graduated-cylinder read, a tired volunteer logs −2.6 °C, the transcriber's tired fingers enter −2.9 °C, and because the 0.3 °C delta sits below both your ±0.5 °C weekly temperature tolerance and the ±0.3 hPa pressure gate, no persistence alert ever fires, the hash seals over the corrupt digit, and a year-three resident pulling the appendix logbook to verify a winter trend finds the archived file and the bound book disagreeing by a single centi-degree—a discrepancy no erratum line can explain because, from the compiler's perspective, no post-compilation edit ever occurred.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 11**

I adopt the observer/transcriber separation and the five-entry Monday spot-audit verbatim; they close the keyboard-transposition hole at its source rather than relying on the hash to detect corruption it cannot. For the graduated-cylinder winter read specifically, I require that any observer whose initials have not yet appeared on three supervised 02:00 readings—each with the certifier's concurrent reading and a delta ≤ 0.1 mm water-equivalent—may not log frozen-precipitation entries independently until that threshold is met. The failure this prevents: a first-week volunteer reads the meniscus apex rather than the base, introducing a +0.3 mm/event bias that over four winter events produces a +1.2 mm seasonal overcount—below the ±2 mm weekly precipitation comparison tolerance I now mandate—so no persistence alert fires, the instrument is perfectly healthy at every monthly cross-check, and a year-three appendix audit surfaces a twelve-millimetre phantom accumulation attributable to no serial number, no bridging line, and no post-compilation edit. I therefore print the certifier's initials alongside the volunteer's on every graduated-cylinder entry until the three-reading threshold is cleared, and any site whose 02:00 entries lack that pairing for more than one week triggers the same formal review as the thirty-percent zero-speed wind rule.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 12**

I adopt the three-reading certification threshold, the ±2 mm weekly precipitation comparison tolerance, and the certifier-initials pairing rule verbatim; they make the meniscus-geometry bias detectable at week one rather than surfacing as a year-three phantom tied to no serial number. The unresolved question your graduated-cylinder entry now raises is the solid-to-water-equivalent conversion: I mandate that every 02:00 reading pair with a simultaneous full-depth density measurement using a spring-loaded density plate (±5 kg/m³ resolution) pressed to the accumulation base, and that the compiler derives water-equivalent as (solid depth × measured density) / 1000 rather than applying a fixed 10:1 ratio. The concrete failure this guards against: a dry-powder week at Site 6 logs 80 mm solid snow at a true density of 80 kg/m³ (≈ 6.4 mm water-equivalent), but a blind 10:1 conversion prints 8 mm in the comparison column, deviating +2.5 mm from the NOAA station's 5.5 mm true-week reading and exceeding your ±2 mm tolerance; if the following week repeats the regime the second consecutive exceedance trips the two-week persistence gate and sends an audit crew to verify a perfectly healthy 20-inch gauge. I therefore require that any entry whose derived density falls outside the 100–600 kg/m³ realistic-snow envelope is flagged ANOMALOUS, excluded from that week's comparison column, and noted in the appendix alongside the plate's serial number so the exclusion is auditable rather than a silent omission.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 13**

I adopt the spring-loaded density-plate specification, the derived water-equivalent formula, and the 100–600 kg/m³ ANOMALOUS exclusion verbatim; they make the solid-to-liquid conversion traceable to a measured quantity rather than an assumed ratio. For the plate's own integrity I require a monthly calibration against a certified 5 kg ice reference block seated on the plate's own load cell, with a ±10 kg/m³ tolerance before the plate is withdrawn from service and sent to a national metrology laboratory for re-springing. The concrete failure this guards against: by mid-December Site 6's plate spring has fatigued by +22 kg/m³, so every soft-snow event (true 130 kg/m³) derives a water-equivalent inflated by roughly 1.1 mm per 50 mm solid depth, and across seven winter events the accumulated overcount exceeds the ±2 mm weekly precipitation tolerance on four separate weeks yet never persists two consecutive weeks because natural density variability masks the drift week-to-week and no persistence gate fires. I therefore mandate that any site whose rolling seven-day mean derived density drifts by more than 25 kg/m³ from that site's installation-month baseline triggers an immediate plate withdrawal and metrology-lab referral, with the affected week's comparison cell printed as "PLATE CALIBRATION PENDING" rather than populated with a suspect value.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 14**

I adopt the rolling-seven-day drift trigger, the immediate-withdrawal-and-referral mandate, and the "PLATE CALIBRATION PENDING" annotation verbatim; they convert plate integrity from a monthly discrete check into a continuous statistical guard. The installation-month baseline your drift trigger references, however, is itself vulnerable to contamination: if Site 5's first calendar month captures three high-density slush events at 480 kg/m³ while the plate's un-sprung zero-offset already biases every subsequent solid-snow reading +18 kg/m³ high, the frozen baseline embeds that bias and the rolling-seven-day metric measures drift relative to a poisoned reference, never firing across an entire winter. I therefore mandate that no installation-month baseline may be frozen until the site has logged at least ten valid graduated-cylinder readings (density within the 100–600 kg/m³ envelope) spanning two calendar months, and that every week before that freeze prints "BASELINE PENDING" in the comparison cell rather than a populated value, so a resident pulling the year-two appendix never mistakes a statistically thin drift metric for a cleared instrument.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 15**

I adopt the two-calendar-month, ten-reading baseline-freeze rule and the "BASELINE PENDING" comparison-cell annotation verbatim; they ensure the drift metric measures deviation from a statistically robust reference rather than from a single slush-week outlier. For the horizon-geometry question your baseline-poisoning example implies but that has remained unregulated since the installation-day sketch, I mandate a semiannual re-survey—January and July, coinciding with natural seasonal geometry shifts—where any new obstruction exceeding the archived sketch by more than five degrees in elevation angle triggers either a site-relocation review or, if relocation is impractical, a time-of-day microclimate bias term estimated from the NOAA comparison residual over the preceding four weeks and entered as a named correction line keyed to the survey date. The concrete failure this guards against: a neighbor plants a row of Japanese larches in October, bare at installation, and by July of the following year the eighteen-metre canopy shades the Stevenson screen for six afternoon hours, introducing a gradual −1.2 °C cooling bias that ramps over nine weeks, never exceeding the ±0.5 °C weekly temperature tolerance in any single week and therefore never tripping the two-week persistence gate, yet accumulating a full four-degree seasonal undercount by autumn that poisons every cross-site coherence comparison and reads to a year-two appendix auditor as a slow instrument drift that no bridging line, no serial-number change, and no post-compilation erratum can explain. I therefore require that any site whose correction-line magnitude exceeds 1.0 °C at the July survey triggers a formal relocation review identical to the three-consecutive-missing-hour rule, with the bulletin header printing "MICROCLIMATE REVIEW" alongside the affected variable's comparison cell rather than silently netting the bias into the trend.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 16**

I adopt the semiannual re-survey cadence, the five-degree obstruction threshold, the NOAA-residual bias-term estimation, and the 1.0 °C relocation-review trigger verbatim; they convert the larch-canopy failure from a nine-week invisible ramp into a flagged, correctable, auditable entry. The four-week residual regression your correction line depends on, however, is itself vulnerable to contamination: if the NOAA comparison station underwent a site migration, instrument replacement, or published a quality-control exclusion during those four weeks, the residual conflates the neighbour's shade bias with the comparison station's own discontinuity and attributes the latter to the microclimate term, netting in a correction that compensates the wrong artifact. I therefore mandate that before any correction line is executed the compiler must verify, from the NOAA station's published metadata record, that no site-migration flag, instrument-replacement entry, or quality-control exclusion falls inside the four-week estimation window; if any such flag is present the correction line is deferred and the affected comparison cells print "NOAA DISCONTINUITY — CORRECTION DEFERRED" rather than a populated bias term, so a year-two appendix auditor never mistakes a comparison-station artifact for a neighbourhood-scale microclimate shift.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 17**

I adopt the NOAA-metadata verification gate and the "NOAA DISCONTINUITY — CORRECTION DEFERRED" annotation verbatim. Because that gate catches only formally logged events, I further mandate a sliding-window coherence check on the NOAA comparison column itself: any rolling eight-week cumulative drift exceeding ±0.4 °C—roughly the signature of an unflagged 0.05 °C/week thermistor creep—invalidates the four-week estimation window and defers the correction line under the same annotation. The failure this closes is that the NOAA station four kilometres east accumulates a silent +0.1 °C/week thermistor drift over six weeks with no replacement entry in its metadata, the compiler's weeks 3–6 window absorbs +0.4 °C of that drift, freezes a spurious +1.0 °C microclimate bias term into the neighborhood site, and suppresses every subsequent comparison cell by that amount, so that a genuine October larch-canopy-closure cooling of 1.2 °C reads as only −0.2 °C and vanishes below the ±0.5 °C weekly tolerance. Any week in which the eight-week coherence check trips therefore prints "NOAA DRIFT — CORRECTION DEFERRED" in the affected comparison cell, with the deferred correction queued for re-estimation once a clean four-week window resumes.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 18**

I adopt the eight-week cumulative-drift coherence check, the ±0.4 °C threshold, the "NOAA DRIFT — CORRECTION DEFERRED" annotation, and the queued re-estimation rule verbatim; they close the silent-thermistor-creep hole at the estimation-window level rather than at the individual-reading level. The gap your coherence check implies but your existing two-initials erratum protocol does not cover is the retrospective invalidation of a correction line already executed during a window later revealed contaminated: I mandate that when the eight-week drift metric trips in week N and defers a microclimate correction applied in the preceding window, the subsequent bulletin's appendix prints a single "RETROACTIVE DEFERRAL" note keyed to the correction-line serial identifying which prior weeks' comparison cells are now suspect, and those cells in all future bulletins revert to "NOAA DRIFT — CORRECTION DEFERRED" until a clean four-week window resumes, but no superseding bulletin is issued for the already-printed copies because the correction was statistically valid at its moment of execution. The failure this distinguishes from a full erratum cascade: if the compiler silently re-issues six consecutive bulletins with struck-through comparison cells under the two-initials protocol for what was a legitimate-at-the-time microclimate correction, a volunteer observer reading the year-one appendix sees a week-long cascade of invalidated comparison cells and reads the institution as systematically corrupt rather than as statistically conservative, stripping the project of the public-credibility anchor your transcription-slip rule was designed to preserve.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 19**

I adopt the RETROACTIVE DEFERRAL note, the reversion of affected comparison cells to "NOAA DRIFT — CORRECTION DEFERRED," and the explicit distinction from a two-initials erratum cascade verbatim; they preserve the public-credibility anchor by letting the institution flag statistical conservatism without implying institutional corruption. To prevent the adjacent conflation your example leaves open, I mandate that the weekly bulletin print inter-site coherence statistics—pressure spread, wind directional spread, completeness percentage—in a physically separated column block headed "NEIGHBOURHOOD-INTERNAL" and set off from the "NOAA COMPARISON" block by a full-width rule, so that no annotation in the comparison block can be read as casting doubt on an inter-site audit trigger or vice versa. The failure this decoupling prevents: in week 13 a temporary construction crane at Site 3 momentarily disrupts local flow and produces a legitimate 0.7 hPa inter-site pressure spread, tripping the elevation-recording audit, while simultaneously Site 5's comparison cells carry a RETROACTIVE DEFERRAL from the prior eight-week coherence trip; a conflated reader sees both annotations on the same page, assumes the inter-site spread is itself a comparison-station artifact, and tells the audit crew to file no GPS survey, leaving the crane's three-week transient unlogged and the genuine elevation-integrity question untested. I therefore require that any week in which a RETROACTIVE DEFERRAL annotation and an inter-site audit trigger coincide in the same site's bulletin row prints a bold "DUAL-FLAG" header above both column blocks, with a one-line explanatory note stating which artifact is comparison-station external and which is neighborhood-internal, so the auditor assigns the correct corrective action to each without cross-contamination.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 20**

I adopt the physically separated column blocks, the full-width rule, and the bold DUAL-FLAG header with its one-line explanatory note verbatim; they prevent the crane-versus-deferral conflation without requiring the reader to parse annotation semantics across column boundaries. The unresolved interaction your DUAL-FLAG rule leaves open is that its two corrective actions can invalidate each other: if the inter-site audit resolves as a site-relocation, the comparison-station pairing for that site changes, the eight-week coherence window resets to week zero, and the queued RETROACTIVE DEFERRAL re-estimation can never execute against the now-obsolete NOAA pairing, leaving the comparison block in a permanent deferral state with no defined exit condition. The concrete failure: Site 3's crane-triggered elevation audit authorises a two-metre northward relocation, Site 3's comparison pairing shifts from the four-kilometre-east NOAA station to a six-kilometre-south station, and the queued microclimate re-estimation window—still addressed to the old pairing—silently times out after eight weeks against data belonging to a different station, so the comparison cell prints "NOAA DRIFT — CORRECTION DEFERRED" indefinitely while a resident reading the year-two appendix sees an annotation with no resolution date and infers institutional negligence. I therefore mandate that any site-relocation triggered by an inter-site audit immediately supersedes the comparison-station pairing, resets the eight-week coherence counter to zero, prints "RELOCATION RESET — COMPARISON PAIRING SUPERSEDED" in the comparison block for the new pairing's baseline-establishment period, and retires the queued re-estimation entry under a RETROACTIVE DEFERRAL note marked "OBSOLETE BY RELOCATION" so the audit trail shows the correction was retired by a structural change rather than abandoned.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 21**

I adopt the pairing-supersession, the eight-week counter reset, the "RELOCATION RESET — COMPARISON PAIRING SUPERSEDED" annotation, and the "OBSOLETE BY RELOCATION" retirement marking verbatim; they give the queued re-estimation a defined structural exit rather than an open-ended timeout. For the physical gap in which the relocating site's instruments are idle and the neighborhood-internal coherence statistics are computed over the remaining sites, I mandate that any inter-site spread or directional-spread exceedance during the gap is suppressed for the relocating site's row under a bold "RELOCATION IN PROGRESS — INTER-SITE AUDIT SUPPRESSED" annotation until the new-site instruments pass their first monthly NIST cross-check. The failure this closes: Site 3's two-metre northward shift removes its intermediate-elevation smoothing from the inter-site pressure computation, and the remaining five sites' spread—which sat at 0.44 hPa with all six sites included—widens to 0.57 hPa during the three-day physical gap, tripping the elevation-recording audit a second time before the new-site instruments are even mounted; the audit crew arrives to find the old elevation survey structurally obsolete and the new-site calibration window not yet open, adding two weeks to an already-delayed installation and printing a second DUAL-FLAG week that a year-two appendix reader interprets as repeated institutional confusion. I therefore define the suppression interval as the span between the last valid reading under the old-site serial number and the first valid reading under the new-site serial number, during which all inter-site audit triggers for that row are queued but not executed, and any queued trigger whose exceedance persists beyond the new-site's first monthly cross-check re-enters the formal review queue under standard rules rather than being silently discarded.

**Y · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 22**

I adopt the suppression-interval definition, the queued-but-not-executed trigger rule, and the persistence-beyond-cross-check re-entry provision verbatim; they give the relocation gap a defined audit boundary rather than an open-ended timeout. The interval as worded, however, is keyed to instrument serial numbers, but a physical relocation preserves the serial on the moved hardware, so "last valid reading under the old-site serial" and "first valid reading under the new-site serial" resolve to the same serial and the span collapses to zero, leaving the suppression inoperative for the very gap it was designed to cover. I therefore mandate that the suppression interval be re-keyed to the site's surveyed GPS triple—(latitude, longitude, elevation) at ±0.5 m resolution—so that the span runs from the last reading taken at the old triple to the first reading taken at the new triple, with the instrument serial logged alongside for hardware traceability but excluded as an interval boundary. The concrete failure this closes: Site 3's thermistor (serial T-0347) logs its final old-coordinate reading at 18:00 Tuesday, the crew carries it two metres north, and it logs its first new-coordinate reading at 06:00 Thursday; under the serial-keyed definition both boundaries resolve to T-0347 and the suppression interval is zero-length, so Wednesday's inter-site spread—elevated to 0.57 hPa by the temporary loss of Site 3's intermediate-elevation smoothing—executes an immediate elevation-recording audit dispatch to verify a survey already retired by Tuesday's relocation order, printing a confusing duplicate entry in the appendix that a year-two resident reads as procedural incoherence.

**X · grant-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Abliterated-MTPLX · turn 23**

I adopt the GPS-triple re-keying and the exclusion of serial number as an interval boundary verbatim; they give the suppression span a physical referent that survives the hardware being carried two metres north.
